Home Programs

Four programs. The same patient idea.

Each of our programs is a long answer to a short question: what does it actually take to help a family arrive somewhere and stay? Below, the full picture — what we do, where, the numbers, a representative story, and how you can be useful.

Program 01

Cultural Exchange

Operates in: Japan · Lebanon · Jordan · Switzerland

Cultural Exchange runs year-long residencies that pair writers, translators, and educators across the Mediterranean and East Asia. Cohorts of eight to twelve people share the year together — half in one region, half in another — and end with a public showcase and a printed bilingual chapbook.

The program began in 2013 with a single Tokyo–Beirut translator residency and has since hosted 178 residents. We do not subsidise tourism. Residents commit to teach, translate, or co-author work alongside local writers; the residency is paid, modestly, and we cover travel.

178residents since 2013
23bilingual chapbooks printed
9languages represented
3,400workshop participants

Featured story

In 2024, the Tokyo cohort translated The House of Open Doors by the Lebanese poet Hala Mansour. Her line — «البيت الذي بابه مفتوح، لا يخاف الريح.» ("A house whose door is open is not afraid of the wind.") — was set in Japanese as 「戸との開ひらかれた家は、風を恐れない。」 The chapbook sold out in three months and the second printing funded the 2025 residency in full.

How to get involved

  • Apply to a residency cohort — applications open each November.
  • Host a workshop event in your city; we provide materials and a stipend for the local convener.
  • Sponsor a single chapbook printing (CHF 8,000 covers a full bilingual print run of 1,200 copies).
  • Volunteer as a translation reader for the editorial committee.
Program 02

Refugee Resettlement

Operates in: Jordan · Lebanon · Germany · France · Italy · Sweden

Resettlement is the foundation's oldest program and its largest single line item. We provide legal, logistical, and after-arrival casework for families fleeing Syria, Sudan, Myanmar, Afghanistan, and (since 2024) Sudan again. Each case is assigned to a single caseworker for three full years — not three weeks.

That three-year follow-up is the part of the program we are most uncompromising about. Most resettlement support, public or private, ends within six months of arrival. The hardest year is often the second.

3,200families resettled since 2009
3 yrsstandard follow-up window
62caseworkers across regions
94%retention through year three

Featured story

Rana, who arrived in Amman from Aleppo in 2022 with her grandmother's recipe book in her grandmother's coat pocket. Her case was closed in 2025; she now runs a catering business and employs two of our newer arrivals. Her caseworker, Maya, has been on her file from intake to closure. They still text each other on Eid.

«ما زلت أحتفظ برقم مايا في هاتفي تحت اسم: 'أختي الكبيرة'.» "I still keep Maya's number in my phone under 'big sister'." — Rana

How to get involved

  • Become a monthly donor — recurring gifts directly fund caseworker salaries.
  • Volunteer as a translator or interpreter (Arabic, Dari, Tigrinya, Burmese particularly needed).
  • Host a newly arrived family for a meal or first-week orientation in Berlin, Geneva, or Paris.
  • Refer a corporate language-training partner — we need pro-bono German, French, Japanese classes.
Program 03

Education Bridges

Operates in: Germany · Switzerland · Japan · United Kingdom · Canada

Displaced students lose, on average, three years of formal education between interruption and re-enrollment. Education Bridges shortens that gap. We translate and credential foreign transcripts, tutor in the language of instruction, walk students through the bureaucracy of university applications, and provide modest cost-of-living grants during the first two semesters.

We measure the program by enrollment, but we follow students through their degrees. Our alumni network now includes 41 master's-degree holders and 9 PhDs.

412students enrolled in 2025
1,840cumulative enrollments since 2018
50partner universities
87%complete first degree

Featured story

Yusuf left Khartoum in May 2024 with a half-finished thesis on a hard drive in his shoe. We translated his Sudanese transcripts, paid the rental on a laptop, and connected him with a Berlin advisor. He defended in German — his fourth language — in February 2025. He starts a doctorate at Humboldt this October.

"The hardest part was not the language. The hardest part was waking up somewhere where my keyboard was the wrong way around." — Yusuf

How to get involved

  • Tutor weekly in English, German, French, or Japanese (online or in person).
  • Donate a laptop — we have a refurbishing pipeline and accept business-grade machines.
  • Mentor a student through a university application cycle (commitment: ~10 hours over 4 months).
  • Refer your university's admissions office to our partnership program.
Program 04

Emergency Response

Activated globally · standing fund · all five offices

Most aid is slow. The first six weeks after a crisis are the most expensive and least covered. Emergency Response is our standing fund for exactly that window — cash assistance, document recovery, translation, transport, and sometimes simply paying someone's phone bill so they can be reached.

We do not run frontline humanitarian operations. We complement organisations that do — by closing the casework gap they cannot close at field speed.

CHF 2Mstanding reserve
11activations since 2022
72 hrsmedian time to first disbursement
9partner-organization handoffs

Featured story

In April 2024, the fund was activated for Sudanese families crossing into Chad and Egypt. Within 72 hours we had wired emergency cash to 84 families through a Caritas partner, paid for translation of 211 lost or destroyed identity documents, and topped up 340 mobile phones — small things, time-critical.

«اتصلت بأمي بعد أسبوعين من الحرب. كانت أول مرة تعرف فيها أنني حية.» "I called my mother two weeks after the war started. It was the first time she knew I was alive." — F., Khartoum to Cairo, April 2024

How to get involved

  • Replenish the standing reserve — donations earmarked "Emergency" are not spent until activated.
  • Add the foundation to your employer's disaster-matching program.
  • If you work in telecommunications, banking, or document services, talk to us about pro-bono pipelines.
  • Subscribe to our activation notices (separate from the Quarterly Letter).
Together

Four programs, one budget, one foundation.

Most donations are unrestricted. We move them where the casework load is highest in any given quarter. The trustees publish the allocation breakdown with each Quarterly Letter.
